tasks.title: The limit of the permutation test
tasks.statement: An A/B comparison, **{n}** flights per arm, an exact two-sided permutation test on the difference of the means. What is the smallest p it can give (with perfect separation of the arms)?
tasks.solution: The number of splits of 2n numbers into two groups of n is C(2n, n). With perfect separation the observed |difference of the means| is reached only by the two extreme splits (all B below all A and vice versa), so p_min = 2 / C(2n, n): 0.333 at n = 2, 0.100 at n = 3, 0.0286 at n = 4.

tasks.title: The effect in standard errors
tasks.statement: Propwash by flight: the mean of A is **{a}** °/s, the mean of B is **{b}** °/s, the pooled spread s_p = **{s}** °/s, **{n}** flights per arm. Find |Δ|/SE.
tasks.solution: SE = s_p·√(1/n_A + 1/n_B) = s_p·√(2/n) with equal arms; |Δ|/SE = |x̄_B − x̄_A| / SE. A course guideline: the effect is real if this is greater than 2 and the permutation test gave p < 0.05.

tasks.title: How many flights per arm
tasks.statement: An A/A test showed a flight-to-flight spread of the metric of CV = **{cv} %**. The expected effect of the change is **{d} %**. How many flights per arm are needed by the course formula (an integer, taking the limit of the permutation test into account)?
tasks.solution: n ≈ 16·(CV/Δ)² (about an 80 % chance of catching the effect with the “2 SE” rule), rounded up. Fewer than 4 is not allowed: at n ≤ 3 an exact permutation test cannot give p < 0.05. Example: CV 8 %, Δ 15 % → 4.55 → 5.
